The Rhetoric of the Title
RED
Signaled Bolshevism, communism,
and aggressive secularism to a
1920s Western audience.
Used here to brand the Mexican
state as an existential threat to
religion and traditional order.
RED MEXICO: 3 reien of terror
REIGN OF TERROR
Borrowed from the French
Revolution, this phrase
explicitly frames the Mexican
government's actions not as
statecraft, but as
ideological slaughter.
MEXICO
The geographic theater of the
Cristero War (1926-1929), a
brutal struggle between the
anti-clerical Mexican
government and Catholic
peasant militias.

Anatomy of a Visual Satire
The Mexican sculptor Hidalgo portrays Calles for the annual show
of the Society of Independent Artists in New York.
The Face

features strip the General of
his dignity, presenting him
as brutish rather than
commanding.
The Uniform

adorned military garb
highlights the absurdity and
theatricality of his
authoritarian power.

This document is not a neutral historical record. It is a carefully engineered piece
of 1920s culture-war propaganda. By combining inflammatory rhetoric with
international visual satire, McCullagh's book was designed to mobilize English-
speaking, Catholic-sympathetic audiences against the secular Mexican state.
The medium, the message, and its institutional preservation perfectly align.
